title: DocumentToolbar exposes toolbarClassName, control lists, component overrides, and per-button props
content:
The `DocumentToolbar` component accepts these props:

```typescript
type DocumentToolbarProps = {
  document?: PHDocument;                            // Override selected document (falls back to useSelectedDocumentSafe)
  toolbarClassName?: string;                        // Classes for the outer container (merged via twMerge)
  controlsContainerClassName?: string;              // Classes for each controls container (merged via twMerge)
  enabledControls?: DocumentToolbarControlName[];    // Render only this subset of built-in controls
  disabledControls?: DocumentToolbarControlName[];   // Remove built-in controls (takes precedence)
  // Available (8): "undo" | "redo" | "download" | "name" | "update" | "history" | "switchboard" | "close"
  // When both lists are omitted, every built-in control is enabled
  componentOverrides?: ToolbarControlComponents;    // Replace individual built-in controls
  customControls?: CustomToolbarControls;           // Add controls to the "first" | "second" | "third" slot
  toolbarContainer?: ContainerComponent;            // Replace the outer container component
  controlsContainer?: ContainerComponent;           // Replace each controls container component
  children?: ReactNode;                             // Replace the entire toolbar contents
};
```

The type is really a union of two mutually exclusive modes: pass `children` to replace the toolbar contents completely, or omit it to render the built-in controls with the customization props above.

There are **eight** built-in controls, not seven. `DocumentToolbarControlName` is derived structurally — `ArrayElement<typeof documentToolbarControls>`, where `documentToolbarControls` is just the three slot arrays spread in order — so the union is whatever `defaultControlSlots` contains:

```typescript
export const defaultControlSlots = {
  first: ["undo", "redo", "download"],
  second: ["name"],
  third: ["update", "history", "switchboard", "close"],
} as const;
```

`update` defaults into the **`third` slot, as its first item** — so it renders immediately left of `history`. The slot layout is not configurable: there is no `controlSlots` prop, and moving a built-in control means disabling it and re-adding it via `customControls` with an explicit `position`.

The `update` control maps to `ToolbarUpgradeButton` (note the vocabulary split: control key `update`, component `Upgrade`). It is the only control that is conditionally invisible: it calls `useDocumentVersionStatus(document)` from `@powerhousedao/reactor-browser` and returns `null` unless the status has resolved *and* `kind === "upgrade-available"` *and* `canUpgrade` is true. So it is absent in three ordinary cases — status still loading, document already current or unsupported, and no registered upgrade path. Default label is "Update available". On click it does **not** perform the upgrade; it calls `showPHModal({ type: "confirmDocumentUpgrade", documentId })`, and the modal that actually calls `upgradeDocument()` lives in `apps/connect`. Consequence worth knowing: in a Connect-less host that has not registered that modal type, the button renders but clicking it does nothing visible. It also has no loading or disabled state — the base `ToolbarButton` supports `disabled`, but only undo/redo use it.

Two styling entry points, not one: `toolbarClassName` for the outer container and `controlsContainerClassName` for each controls container. There is no `className` prop on `DocumentToolbar` itself.

Styling individual buttons mostly does not need a child-selector workaround. The built-in button controls accept `ToolbarButtonProps` (`document`, `children`, `className`, `onClick`), and **seven of the eight defaults are exported** — `ToolbarUndoButton`, `ToolbarRedoButton`, `ToolbarDownloadButton`, `ToolbarName`, `ToolbarHistoryButton`, `ToolbarSwitchboardButton`, `ToolbarCloseButton` — so each can be restyled directly and dropped back in through `componentOverrides` or `children`.

`ToolbarUpgradeButton` is the exception, and it is a real asymmetry rather than an oversight you can route around. It is not re-exported from the component's `index.ts`, so it is not reachable through the `@powerhousedao/design-system/connect` barrier either, and the package's build only emits a handful of entrypoints, so there is no deep-import escape hatch. `componentOverrides` is typed `Partial<Record<DocumentToolbarControlName, ToolbarControlComponent>>`, so `componentOverrides={{ update: MyButton }}` typechecks fine — **you can replace the update control, but you cannot import its default and wrap it.** Any override must reimplement the version-status check from scratch. Override components receive exactly one prop, `{ document?: PHDocument }`, not the full `ToolbarButtonProps`.

The `enabledControls` / `disabledControls` arrays let you hide/show buttons; restyling or rebehaving them individually goes through `componentOverrides` or a direct button import.

Note that the component's own `README.md` is stale on exactly this point — it still lists seven controls and a `third` slot of `["history", "switchboard", "close"]`. The constants file is authoritative.
